study.title: John 13 The love that humbles itself, the betrayal that is approaching and the denial announced
study.overview: John 13 marks the transition from the public ministry of Jesus to his intimate instruction to the disciples before the cross. The chapter unites three great movements: Jesus washes the disciples' feet as an example of humility and service; Jesus reveals that one of them will betray him, showing that his surrender is not an accident, but part of the fulfillment of the Scriptures; and Jesus ends with the new commandment of love and with the prediction of Peter's denial. The chapter shows Jesus in full awareness of his origin, mission and destiny, governing events even when betrayal and human weakness advance.

outline.title: Jesus washes the feet of the disciples
outline.explanation: Before speaking of his death, Jesus acts with concrete humility: he removes his garments, takes the towel and serves the disciples. Peter resists, but Jesus teaches that communion with him depends on being washed by him. At the same time, Jesus distinguishes the royal cleansing of the disciples from the impurity of the one who would betray him.

outline.title: The example, authority and Scripture
outline.explanation: Jesus interprets his own gesture as a model for the disciples: who calls him a Master and Lord should learn to serve. He claims that the servant is not greater than you and promises bliss to those who practice what they know. Then, he points out that the betrayal of Judas fulfills the Scripture and that receiving the envoys of Jesus is to receive Christ himself and the Father.

outline.title: The betrayal of Judas and the glory of the Son
outline.explanation: Jesus announces in a direct way that one of the twelve will betray him. The beloved disciple, at Peter's request, asks who he is, and Jesus identifies Judas with the wet piece of bread. After that, Satan dominates him more decisively and Judas leaves; then Jesus declares that in his way out and on the way of the cross, the Son of Man will be glorified and God will be glorified in him.

outline.title: The new commandment and the predicted fall of Peter
outline.explanation: Jesus speaks of the brief imminent separation and gives the disciples a new commandment: to love one another as he loved them. This love will be the visible mark of discipleship. Finally, Peter promises allegiance to death, but Jesus announces that he will deny him three times before the cock crows.

study.context: The chapter is located at the last supper of Jesus with the disciples, on the eve of the Passover, according to the notes provided. The notes of Tyndale and Adam Clarke note that John especially highlights the washing-foot and farewell words, in contrast to the other gospels, which record the meal in more detail. The notes also indicate that there is discussion about the exact relationship between the footwash and the moment of the meal, but all agree that the scenario is the last night before the arrest of Jesus. The text emphasizes that Jesus knows in advance his hour, his return to the Father, the betrayal of Judas and the denial of Peter.
study.theology: This chapter presents a high Christology and an ethics of discipleship deeply linked to the cross. Jesus acts with full awareness of his origin and his destiny, and his humiliation in the washing feet does not diminish his authority; on the contrary, he reveals the character of his greatness. The service of Jesus is exemplary: he not only commands to love and serve, but incarnates the pattern that he demands. The purification he offers is necessary for communion with him, which suggests that spiritual cleansing does not depend on human resistance, but on his work. The betrayal of Judas does not nullify Jesus" control over the situation; on the contrary, the chapter shows that human wickedness and the action of Satan operate without escaping the fulfillment of Scripture and the rule of Christ. Finally, mutual love is presented as the disciples" public mark, making brotherly love a visible evidence of belonging to Jesus.

scholarViews.insight: The notes highlight that Jesus is glorified in the events that go to the cross, and that the context is the final supper in which Judas betrays him.
The commentator notes that Jesus concludes his public ministry and proceeds to instruct the disciples in particular, preparing them for their absence and for the care of the community.
The note understands the footwash as a gesture of humility and charity, and highlights that Jesus washed his feet to teach this attitude to the disciples.

questions: What changes in my way of treating others when I take seriously that Jesus, my Lord, served so humblely?
Is there any resistance in me to be washed by Christ - that is, depending on him for my spiritual cleansing and fellowship with him?
Is my love for brothers and sisters in faith visible enough for others to identify that I am a disciple of Jesus?
study.practice: This week, choose a concrete attitude of humble service that no one expects from you: listening to someone attentively, taking on a simple task, asking for forgiveness first or helping without seeking recognition. In doing so, remember that the pattern of Jesus is not only to have to love, but to love serving. Also examine if there are areas in which you, like Peter, trust more in your own strength than in the grace of Christ; pray for a teachable and vigilant heart.
study.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty in the notes about the exact chronological relationship between the lava-foot and the paschal meal, and also about the precise way of understanding the beginning of the episode; therefore, it is not safe to say more than the text and commentators provide. In addition, the notes do not detail all possible symbolic aspects of the lava-foots, so that the interpretation should remain close to the text and the observations cited.
